claims.statement: dynstack derives a dynamic stack's name from the CONTENT of the recipe set, so the same set resolves to the same stack in every repo that asks for it — one image, one pair of volumes, shared — which is what stops ad-hoc `--recipe` composition from multiplying build artifacts.

Both run verbs (`container-run` and `host-run`) resolve their stack through the same `launcher._resolve_stack`, so the two grammars cannot drift: they differ in backend and never in how a stack is chosen (bd harnessed-s84).

`launcher._resolve_stack` calls `_seed_user_default_recipe()` first, because resolution is the step that needs the shipped baseline to exist (a `--recipe` set mints `extends: default`) and one shared call site is what keeps the two backends in step.

Supplying both `--stack` and `--recipe` is rejected with exit 1; supplying neither runs the `--extends` baseline as the stack itself (composing nothing on top of the baseline is a legitimate launch, bd harnessed-jhj), and `--no-extends` with no recipes is rejected because it inherits nothing and there is nothing left to run.

`--extends` defaults to `_EXTENDS_DEFAULT = "default"` only on the DYNAMIC (`--recipe`) path: an authored `--stack foo` returns immediately without consulting `--extends` or folding in any baseline, so an authored stack.yaml does not implicitly extend the baseline.
The derived name carries the base as its first component: `derive_name(["serena"], "default")` yields `default.serena`, distinct from `derive_name(["serena"], None)` which yields `serena`.

`normalize` dedupes and sorts the recipe refs (dropping whitespace-only entries), which is what makes `--recipe a --recipe b` and `--recipe b --recipe a` the same stack; `_normalize_services` does the same for `--service` names.

`_sanitize` is lossy by design: it lowercases, replaces `/` with `-`, folds every run of characters outside `[a-z0-9-]` to `-`, and strips edge `-`s — so `Foo`/`foo` and `foo bar`/`foo-bar` collapse together, and a catalog ref like `fam/var` flattens to `fam-var`.

`derive_name` refuses an empty recipe list (`ValueError: a dynamic stack needs at least one recipe`) and refuses any value whose sanitized form lands in `_RESERVED = {"", ".", ".."}` — an all-unsafe ref like `***` sanitizes to empty and `.`/`..` fold to `-` which the trailing strip removes, so mint would otherwise write into the stacks dir itself or its parent. `.` and `..` stay listed because the check must hold whatever the alphabet is.

`derive_name` appends an 8-hex digest (`-<sha256[:8]>`) whenever the readable join is not a faithful encoding: any ref was sanitized lossily (checked as any difference between original and sanitized, not just `/`), the join exceeded `NAME_MAX` (64), or explicit services were selected; the truncation strips trailing `.`/`-` so the cut cannot leave an illegal separator before the suffix's dash.

The digest is computed from the UNSANITIZED inputs, so two sets that sanitize to the same readable string still hash differently (e.g. `beads/team` mints `beads-team-55bfd6ac` while a recipe literally named `beads-team` mints `beads-team`), and a `\x1f` between the refs group and the services group keeps `(refs=("a","b"), svcs=())` distinct from `(refs=("a",), svcs=("b",))`.

`_JOIN = "."` must be legal in an OCI image tag AND impossible for `_sanitize` to emit: the name is interpolated into the podman tag `harnessed-<harness>-<stack>:latest` (`layout._derived_image`), so it must satisfy the OCI name-component grammar, and if a sanitized ref could contain the separator, `["a.b","c"]` and `["a","b.c"]` would both join to `a.b.c` with neither flagged lossy — a silent collision onto one manifest, one image and one pair of volumes.

Because `.` and `_` are the only tag-legal separators, `_sanitize`'s output alphabet is narrowed to `[a-z0-9-]` with `.` reserved for the join; folding `_` and `.` into `-` also closes the leading-separator hole, since a ref like `_foo` or `.foo` would otherwise survive intact and produce a component starting with a separator, which the grammar forbids.

Services are the third input to a dynamic stack's identity alongside the base and the recipe set, and they never appear in the readable join (that would bloat every name for a rarely-used escape hatch), so the digest is their only carrier — `svcs` being non-empty therefore forces a digest, while an empty service list must not put one on the common case.

`services` MUST be passed to BOTH `derive_name` and `mint` by every caller: deriving without them computes a different name than `mint()` does, so the preexisting-stack check would inspect the wrong path, and omitting them from either call lets two different service selections mint over each other's manifest and share one image and volume pair. `launcher._resolve_stack` passes `services=list(service)` to both.

`mint` writes (or refreshes) the manifest at `<generated_catalog_root>/stacks/<name>/stack.yaml`, rendering the sorted deduped recipe list, an `extends:` key only when a base was given (`--no-extends` emits none), and `services: []` when no services were selected.

`mint` is idempotent and mtime-honest: identical inputs rewrite identical bytes and the file is written only when the content differs, so a repeat launch does not perturb the staleness check and the file's mtime tracks real change.
Being machine-made is expressed by LOCATION under the generated catalog root, not by a manifest key: a stack manifest rejects unknown fields unconditionally, so `generated` is a comment, not a key.

`mint` REFUSES (raises `ValueError`) rather than shadows when the derived name collides with an authored stack: the generated root is deliberately last in `paths.catalog_roots()` precedence, so an authored stack of the same name wins resolution and `find_in_catalog` would hand both build and launch the authored manifest while the minted one sat ignored — `run` would silently execute something the user did not ask for (reported on PR #176). A pre-existing manifest under the generated root is not a collision; minting over it is the refresh it exists for.

`launcher._resolve_stack` serializes the is_file→mint sequence for one derived name under `launcher._mint_lock(derived)`, an exclusive flock on `<generated>/stacks/{derived}.lock` — a SIBLING of the stack dir so it survives an rmtree of the guarded directory, released before `_resolve_stack` returns and never held across a build (#287).

`derive_name` is pure computation and its return value IS the lock key, so calling it outside the lock is correct by design — issue #287, reviewed and confirmed; moving it inside would deadlock on a key that does not exist yet.

`_resolve_stack` returns `(name, minted_dir)` where `minted_dir` is non-None only when THIS call created the manifest — the `preexisting` probe is read under the lock before mint — so an authored stack and a dynamic one whose manifest already existed both yield None and are not the caller's to delete.

`container-run` calls `_build_stack` immediately on the `--recipe` form (a freshly minted stack has no assembled profile and everything below hard-errors without one), unconditionally because the build is fingerprint-gated downstream and deliberately not skipped under `--create-aoe-only`; on failure it rmtree's `minted_dir`, because a stack that never built lingers in the catalog, appears in `harnessed list`, and no GC reclaims it (`volume-gc` keys on volumes, and a stack that never built owns none). A pre-existing manifest is left alone.

`host-run` removes `minted_dir` on a non-zero `typer.Exit` or unexpected exception but NOT on `typer.Exit(0)`: exit 0 is `--create-aoe-only` succeeding after writing an aoe row whose recorded command names this manifest, so deleting it would manufacture precisely the dead-on-arrival row the flow avoids. Host mode has no build to fail, but `_launch_host` assembles in-process and a `SchemaError`/`CollisionError` from a bad recipe set reaches the cleanup.
`host-run` mints exactly like `container-run` but performs no image build even for a minted recipe set: `_launch_host` assembles in-process on every launch.
`_resolve_stack` converts the `ValueError`/`OSError` raised by `derive_name` or `mint` (reserved component, empty recipe set, authored-stack collision) into a one-line error and exit 1.

A real `stack.yaml` is minted rather than passing a recipe list straight to the assembler because profile location, volume labels, staleness checks, `harnessed list`, and BOTH garbage collectors are already keyed on "a stack that resolves in the catalog"; minting makes all of them work unchanged, while skipping it would mean teaching five subsystems about a new kind of thing.

Both garbage collectors key orphan detection on catalog resolution: `host-gc` marks a host config dir an orphan when `find_in_catalog("stacks", <name>)/stack.yaml` is not a file, and `volume-gc` reads the stack name off the volume's `harnessed.stack` label (never by parsing the volume name) and applies the same test — which is what makes a minted stack GC-eligible and authored-stack-protected through the identical mechanism, with no special case for generated stacks in either collector.

`harnessed list` enumerates generated stacks alongside authored ones because `paths.list_catalog_stacks()`/`list_catalog(kind)` walk every catalog root including the generated root, deduping by name with the overlay first.

The generated catalog root is `$XDG_DATA_HOME/harnessed/generated` (XDG DATA, not the user's `~/.config/harnessed/catalog` overlay): mixing generated manifests into the overlay would mean `harnessed list` cannot tell them apart and a regenerated file silently clobbers a hand edit; it is included in `catalog_roots()` only when it exists, so a user who never ran a dynamic launch sees exactly the previous two roots.

The content-derived name is what makes the same recipe set across multiple repos share one derived image (`harnessed-<harness>-<stack>:latest` via `layout._derived_image`) and one volume pair (`harnessed-cfg-<harness>-<stack>` / `harnessed-tools-<harness>-<stack>`).

A content-derived stack name is what can push an instance name past Linux's 64-character HOST_NAME_MAX, and podman derives the hostname from the pod name, so `harnessed-omp-default.beads-team.serena.superpowers-f6eb0941-59258991` (69 chars) killed every launch with `sethostname: Invalid argument` on the infra container until `paths.container_hostname` began truncating the middle — keeping the `harnessed-<harness>-` head and the whole trailing project hash, purely cosmetic because nothing keys on the hostname.

`aoe.command_for` records the RESOLVED stack name as `--stack <derived-name>`, never the user's original argv: a dynamic stack is minted into the generated catalog root before this is called, so `--stack <derived-name>` replays it exactly and one canonical form serves every verb that reaches there — a row records the same shape whether the user typed `--stack` or a `--recipe` set.

The derived name is NOT parseable back into recipe refs, and `aoe._composed_recipes` therefore reads the RAW manifest rather than `load_stack` or the name: `derive_name` joins on `.` after sanitizing and appends a digest when lossy or over-long, so the single recipe `beads/team` mints as `default.beads-team-55bfd6ac`, and splitting that on `.` yields `beads-team-55bfd6ac`, which is neither the recipe nor recoverable. It also uses location (under the generated root) to decide a stack is machine-made — an authored stack returns `[]` — and a missing, unreadable or malformed manifest costs only the delta, never a failed launch.

`ssh_keys` (private-key mounts) are always dropped for a generated stack: `mint` never writes an `ssh_keys:` key, and a generated stack resolves under the generated root rather than the user's overlay, so `credmounts._stack_from_overlay` is False and `_trusted_ssh_keys` drops any keys inherited through `extends:` with a warning — private-key mounting is the key owner's decision, honored only from the user's own overlay catalog.

The shipped `catalog/stacks/default/stack.yaml` exists so the documented `--extends` default works out of the box: until it existed the repo shipped no `default` stack, so a fresh install running a `--recipe` launch failed on `extends: 'default' — no such stack`. It is deliberately minimal (one recipe, no services, no policy fields) because a shipped baseline that set `permissions:` or turned on credential forwarding would silently apply that policy to every dynamic stack on every install; authoring `~/.config/harnessed/catalog/stacks/default/stack.yaml` replaces it wholesale because the overlay wins the name clash.

`--service` selections only enter stack identity on the mint path: with `--stack`, or on the bare baseline launch, `_resolve_stack` returns before the service list is read, so those services are dropped rather than applied (not an error).

The OCI-tag-grammar constraint is enforced by construction rather than by launch-time checking because podman rejects a bad tag only at build time and the test suite runs no podman — so a character legal in a directory name but illegal in a tag would pass every unit assertion and die only in a real `podman build`; the live contract tests behind `HARNESSED_PODMAN=1` are the only layer that can observe it.
